title: Playing Bayesian games better with separable quantum states than with any classical correlation
authors: Yaqing Xy Wang, Giannicola Scarpa, Andreas Winter
abstract: Bayesian games, also known as games of incomplete information, are a fruitful arena for exploring the impact of correlations on a set of independent agents (players) via the game equilibria to which they give rise. It was realised some time ago that quantum states shared between the players can lead to new and beneficial equilibria, compared to classical correlation. While until now examples of this effect required an entangled state, here we show that even separable states can create new, genuinely quantum equilibria in games, that are advantageous with respect to all classically correlated equilibria. This shows that non-classical correlations beyond entanglement are indeed a resource, even in otherwise entirely classical situations. Our result brings quantum advantage in games significantly closer to possible realisation.
summary: This theoretical paper explores quantum advantages in Bayesian games by comparing equilibria derived from classical versus separable quantum correlations. It proves that these local quantum states can achieve better outcomes than any classically correlated strategy, even when the game involves conflicting interests. This advances the understanding of non-classical resources beyond simple entanglement.
main_problem: The research investigates how different types of correlations (classical vs. quantum) affect the equilibria achieved by independent agents in Bayesian games of incomplete information.
main_result: The paper demonstrates that even separable quantum states can generate new, genuinely quantum equilibria in competitive Bayesian games that yield higher social welfare than any equilibrium achievable using only classical correlations.
method: The analysis uses game theory frameworks (Nash, Correlated Equilibria) combined with quantum information tools to compare the set of possible joint probability distributions derived from local vs. quantum measurements.
model_or_system: The model is a general Bayesian game involving multiple players and incomplete information about their types. The correlation structure is modeled using quantum states (separable vs. entangled) acting on the players' shared Hilbert space.
key_observables: Social Welfare (SW), expected utility for individual players, and the comparison of equilibrium sets ($	ext{Corr}(G)$ vs. $	ext{QuSEP}(G)$).
important_parameters: The structure of the game itself, including payoff functions and prior distributions $p(t)$. Specific examples use parameters related to CHSH inequalities.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that separable quantum correlations are sufficient to demonstrate a quantum advantage in competitive settings, moving beyond previous reliance on full entanglement.
figures_summary: Figures compare various equilibrium scores (e.g., CHSH scores) against classical limits ($ eta(G)$), showing separations between correlated and Nash equilibria when quantum strategies are employed.
paper_structure: The paper builds by first establishing the general framework of Bayesian games, then comparing correlation types (classical vs. quantum), and finally applying these concepts to specific examples like modified CHSH games to quantify the advantage.
why_interesting: While not directly about AMO systems, the rigorous mathematical tools developed for quantifying non-local correlations in game theory are highly relevant to understanding resource theories in open quantum systems or multipartite entanglement verification.
